question: How does hardened oil — hydrogenation, the factory ship, the plantation — turn the world's fats into one industrial system, and where does the fear of fat begin?
thesis: From 1900 to 1960 fat becomes a chemical, corporate and strategic commodity. Hydrogenation lets any liquid oil be hardened into lard or margarine; Lever, Unilever and Procter & Gamble build supply chains from palm, coconut, whale and soy; two world wars and a depression turn fats into a matter of tariffs, rationing and glycerine; and from 1952 the fear of dietary fat begins.

big_ideas.title: Hardening makes oils interchangeable
big_ideas.text: Normann’s patents of 1902 and Kayser’s process, sold to Procter & Gamble as Crisco, turn liquid oils into solid fats. Margarine’s fats change from coconut to cottonseed to soy within a generation, Manchurian and American soy come into play, and in India vanaspati grows from a ghee additive to 43,000 tons a year.

big_ideas.title: Firms build global supply chains
big_ideas.text: Lever leases the Solomon Islands for 999 years, is refused West Africa and turns to the Congo, opens soap works at Apapa and merges with the Margarine Union in 1929. Meanwhile Southeast Asia’s palm plantations overtake Nigeria, helped by a hybrid palm from Kamerun.

big_ideas.title: Whale oil becomes a strategic and industrial fat
big_ideas.text: The grenade harpoon and stern slipway let factory ships kill the fast whales, the First World War makes whale oil contraband for its glycerine, Lever buys the world’s output in 1919, the 1930–31 season is a slaughter, and a convention tries to limit it.

big_ideas.title: Wars and the slump make fat a state matter
big_ideas.text: Copra is war material, a depression glut brings tariffs and imperial preference at Ottawa, Washington taxes coloured margarine until 1949, and Turkey’s duties end the fat imports. The two wars repeat the same pattern of rationing and cut-off oilseeds.

big_ideas.title: The fear of fat begins
big_ideas.text: In 1952 Keys sets out the diet–heart hypothesis, Kummerow warns of trans fats in rats in 1957–58, and in 1961 the American Heart Association first recommends a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet to the public.

threads.title: Hardening and the new fats
threads.claim: A laboratory process frees the fat industry from the animal and gives it soy, cottonseed and coconut.

beats.text: Cottonseed oil, sold as Wesson Oil, holds back American soy until 1915, and a Decatur crushing plant opens in 1922.
Normann’s hydrogenation patents and a first hardening plant make liquid oils solid.
Procter & Gamble’s team turns Kayser’s technique into Crisco, an ‘all-vegetable’ lard.
Manchurian soybeans reach Europe, the first whole shipments reported about 1908.
Crisco is launched nationally to persuade housewives to replace lard.
A British advertisement sells ‘Nut Lard’, coconut fat, as better than lard or butter.
US margarine moves from coconut oil, up to 75 per cent of raw materials, to cottonseed to soy.
Blue Band margarine is advertised in the Netherlands as ‘just like the best butter’.
Vanaspati sales grow from a ghee additive to 43,065 tons after India’s tariff of 1931–32.

threads.title: The oil palm moves to Southeast Asia
threads.claim: From four seedlings in Java to the world’s main palm-oil exporter in under a century.

beats.text: Four oil-palm seedlings reach the botanical gardens at Bogor as ornamentals.
In Kamerun the Germans identify the thin-shelled palm later called Tenera, which gives much more oil.
Plantings in Sumatra and Malaya grow from a few thousand hectares to tens of thousands.
The Netherlands East Indies replace Nigeria as the world’s major palm-oil exporter.

threads.title: Lever and Unilever build the supply chain
threads.claim: A soap maker secures its oil by buying islands, forests and factories, and ends as a multinational.

beats.text: Lever leases the Solomon Islands for 999 years for coconut plantations.
Refused West African land by the Colonial Office, Lever turns to the Congo.
Lever Brothers sets up the Huileries du Congo Belge.
Northern Nigeria’s groundnuts take off when the railway reaches Kano, on local initiative.
Lever’s Apapa soap works in Nigeria grow from 264 tons in 1924 to over 3,000 in 1929.
Atatürk’s duties end Turkey’s fat imports, and a Unilever survey finds a market for margarine.
Lever Brothers and the Margarine Union merge as Unilever.

threads.title: Whale oil and the other marine fats
threads.claim: Industrial whaling kills the whales that earlier methods could not catch, and the First World War and the soap trade make it strategic.

beats.text: Foyn’s grenade harpoon and the factory ship let whalers take the fast rorquals.
Whale oil, a source of glycerine and so of explosives, becomes contraband.
The Pacific sardine fishery booms for about twenty years and then collapses.
Lever buys the world’s whale-oil production and the Southern Whaling Company.
A stern slipway lets whales be processed anywhere, and the 1930–31 season is a slaughter.
A Geneva convention, amended in London in 1937, sets minimum sizes and seasons.

threads.title: Tariffs, taxes and war
threads.claim: Governments tax, protect and ration fats, and each war and slump reshuffles who supplies them.

beats.text: Washington puts ten cents a pound on coloured margarine and almost nothing on white.
The Pacific coconut becomes war material for its glycerine.
The depression brings a glut of oils and fats, with whale-oil output doubled.
Ottawa’s imperial preference puts oils and fats behind imperial tariffs.
The second war for fats repeats the first, with rationing and cut-off oilseeds.
Washington repeals the tax on coloured margarine.
The International Olive Oil Council is founded under UN auspices.

threads.title: The fear of fat begins
threads.claim: Within ten years a hypothesis about fat and the heart becomes official advice.

beats.text: Keys presents his diet–heart hypothesis at Mount Sinai, from fat intake to cholesterol to heart disease.
Kummerow shows trans fatty acids depositing in rat tissues.
The American Heart Association publishes the first official recommendation of a low-fat, low-cholesterol diet.

turning_points.text: Normann patents the hydrogenation of oils.
Crisco is launched to replace lard.
Lever founds the Huileries du Congo Belge.
Whale oil becomes contraband for its glycerine.
Lever buys the world’s whale oil.
The stern slipway makes factory ships global.
Ottawa puts oils and fats behind imperial tariffs.
Southeast Asia overtakes Nigeria in palm oil.
The AHA recommends a low-fat diet.

text: The makers and sellers: Normann’s hardening patents, Lever’s purchase of the world’s whale oil, Unilever, Blue Band and ‘Nut Lard’, the factory ship from Vestfold, and the International Olive Oil Council ([[te1]], [[ec1]], [[ec3]], [[e2]], [[e3]], [[te3]], [[o5]]).

One entry: Turkey in 1939, where Atatürk’s duties had destroyed the import trade in edible fats and a Unilever survey found a market for margarine and ghee substitute, with a local firm claiming three-quarters of organised oil sales ([[ec16]]).

Southeast Asia overtakes Nigeria in palm oil, with Sumatra and Malaya’s plantations; Manchurian soy goes to Europe; and India’s vanaspati grows from a ghee additive to 43,000 tons a year ([[ec6]], [[ec10]], [[ec7]], [[x1]], [[ec12]]).

Lever is refused West Africa and turns to the Congo; the Tenera palm is bred at Yangambi and in Cameroon ([[ec9]], [[ec8]], [[te4]]); Lever’s soap works at Apapa make Nigeria a manufacturer; northern Nigeria’s groundnut exports take off with the railway to Kano, on Hausa traders’ initiative ([[ec14]], [[ec15]]); and, run entirely on its own terms, the LoDagaa and Gonja of northern Ghana gather and process shea nuts into an oil that is cooking fat at home and a traded skin pomade once it reaches Ashanti country, its harvest timed to the Bagre ceremonies ([[ec18]]). Apart from the groundnut and shea entries these are company histories; African growers mostly appear as labour and as a market.

Crisco and Ivorydale, the colour tax and its repeal, the soy crush at Decatur, margarine’s changing fats and the first diet–heart warnings ([[te2]], [[e1]], [[o1]], [[o4]], [[ec5]], [[ec4]], [[th1]], [[th2]], [[th3]]).

Two entries: the Pacific coconut as glycerine and war material, with the plantations of the Philippines and Indonesia taken in 1942, and Lever’s 999-year lease of the Solomon Islands ([[ec11]], [[ec13]]).

The wars for glycerine and for fats, imperial preference, the whaling convention, the Antarctic slaughter and the glut of the Depression ([[c1]], [[c2]], [[o2]], [[o3]], [[ec2]], [[w1]]). Fish oil and the Pacific sardine fishery add the other marine fat ([[ec17]]).

sources.intro: A good documentary base on hardening and margarine (Aoyagi, van Stuyvenberg, Dyer, Fieldhouse, Jones), whaling (Ellis) and palm (Kiple, Zuckerman, Martin, Pye); a journalist's account of the nutrition story.
main: Aoyagi, Hunt in van Stuyvenberg, Dyer et al. and Schleifer ([[te1]], [[te2]], [[e1]]); van Stuyvenberg ([[o1]], [[o4]], [[ec4]], [[e2]]).
Ellis ([[c1]], [[te3]], [[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[o3]]); Jones and Fieldhouse ([[ec3]], [[ec8]]); Kiple, Zuckerman, Pye, Martin ([[ec6]], [[ec7]], [[ec9]], [[ec10]], [[te4]]).
Fieldhouse, *Unilever Overseas*, for India, Nigeria, the Solomon Islands and Turkey ([[ec12]], [[ec14]], [[ec13]], [[ec16]]); Hopkins for the Kano groundnuts ([[ec15]]).
Kiple (O’Keefe) for fish oil and the Pacific sardine fishery ([[ec17]]).
contested: Keys's hypothesis and the AHA's advice ([[th1]], [[th3]]); Kummerow's warning ([[th2]]).
Whether Crisco founded the trans-fat age ([[te2]]); the date hardening reached the US ([[ec4]]).
Kiple's soy account dates a tariff to 1923, which looks wrong, and the folio does not repeat it ([[ec5]]).
gaps: Africa and India in the age of hardening, the German and Japanese fat economies, and olive oil under the Spanish and Italian regimes are missing.
No source for the first hardened butter substitutes in Britain, or for oil-seed crushing in India.
Latin America beyond the United States has no entry; the Near East has one (Turkey in 1939), and Africa beyond Lever’s concessions, Nigerian soap and groundnuts is missing.

how_to_read: Read the thesis and the big ideas first, then the threads: each runs in date order and points to the entries that carry it. Entries that no thread needs are still reached through the regional picture and the lists.

Read *Technology* first: three machines (hydrogenation, the factory ship, the Tenera palm) reshape three fat chains. *Economy* and *Order* show who gained and who taxed them; *Thought* marks the start of the nutrition fight.
Several tiers are CONTESTED or flagged: Teicholz is a polemical source on the diet–heart story, and van Stuyvenberg's dating of US hardening conflicts with the Crisco date.

The *picture by region* counts the 36 entries: Europe 7, Near East 1, Far East 5, Africa 5, Americas 9, Oceania 2, Worldwide 7. North America and Europe make and regulate fat, Africa and Southeast Asia supply it, and the Pacific supplies copra.
